segments.title: How ships in ordinary gave navies more depth
segments.summary: The traditional reserve system kept uncommissioned ships available and reassigned aging vessels to secondary roles as frontline standards changed.
segments.body: A ship could remain in ordinary for years before receiving a crew when the fleet needed more hulls. This system separated ownership of useful hulls from the peacetime cost of keeping every one commissioned. Once HMS Warrior no longer dominated the battle line, her surviving capabilities still suited cruiser, overseas-presence, and secondary duties rather than immediate disposal. A warship's remaining mission matters more than how it compares with the newest ship in its former category.

evidence.note: The lecture defines ships in ordinary and follows Warrior's transition into less demanding roles.

segments.title: Why modern naval thinking discounts reserve ships
segments.summary: Treaty limits, rapid wartime technological change, and Cold War nuclear timelines weakened the older assumption that navies should retain large reserve fleets.
segments.body: Interwar treaties removed much of the overage tonnage that larger navies had traditionally retained. After 1945, visible technological change and planning for wars expected to turn nuclear within days reinforced the preference for cutting-edge systems. Those assumptions made older ships appear both too dated to fight and too slow to activate. This narrowed the test of usefulness: an old platform need not defeat its newest counterpart if it can still perform fire support or another lower-threat mission. The comparison with old tanks used as mobile fire support shows how a platform can remain valuable without serving at the point of the main attack.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke connects treaty restrictions and nuclear-war assumptions to the decline of reserve-fleet thinking.

segments.title: Bramble-class ships challenge modern ideas of old age
segments.summary: HMS Rattler and other Bramble-class vessels show that ships approaching thirty years old could still be useful when their duties matched their surviving capabilities.
segments.body: HMS Rattler and the Bramble class raise the question of whether a 28-year-old ship was exceptionally old by wartime standards. Modern frigates have also remained in service for roughly three decades, so calendar age alone says little about usefulness. Patrol, presence, and secondary duties place different demands on a hull than battle-fleet service. The comparison directs viewers to assess material condition, crew availability, and mission fit before treating age as a reason for disposal.

evidence.note: The lecture identifies Rattler and the Bramble class as useful World War I ships about 28 years old and compares that age with modern frigate service lives.

segments.title: A crew shortage need not end a ship's career
segments.summary: World War I reservists crewed older ships for escort, training, and presence duties, suggesting that a temporary personnel shortage need not require disposal.
segments.body: The lecture contrasts current Royal Navy crewing pressures with a period when reservists activated ships without modern simulators or distributed training. Type 26 and Type 31 crews begin forming before launch, so new construction can draw on scarce personnel before a ship enters service. Modern civilian experience with computerized controls is no substitute for naval training, but it broadens the pool from which technical familiarity can be developed. A temporary shortage need not require selling or scrapping a structurally useful ship, especially after money has already been spent on refit. HMS Protector and similar vessels handled training, escort, lighter, and flag-showing work while scarce modern combatants concentrated elsewhere. Their crews and missions show that reserve activation did not require every old hull to become a first-line combatant.

evidence.note: The transcript discusses current crewing pressures, reservist skills, and Protector's changing utility.

segments.title: HMS Protector outlived her original gunboat role
segments.summary: The flat-iron gunboat HMS Protector moved from Boxer Rebellion service to World War I activation and lighter duties during World War II.
segments.body: Protector was a flat-iron gunboat that had served in China during the Boxer Rebellion before returning from reserve in 1914. By 1943 she was again in commission as a lighter and was subsequently taken over by the Americans. Neither duty required her to match a modern warship, yet the hull continued to carry out work that otherwise would have consumed another vessel or shore capacity. Her career turns the lecture's abstract reserve argument into a concrete example of a ship delivering useful service across very different conflicts and roles.

evidence.note: The lecture traces Protector from Boxer Rebellion service through 1914 reactivation to lighter work and American control in 1943.

segments.title: Reserve mobilisation deters war and adds convoy depth
segments.summary: Activating reserves can signal political seriousness before war and provide adequate escorts where top-tier combatants are unnecessary.
segments.body: Britain began activating reserves before the declarations of war in both 1914 and 1939, making mobilization part of deterrence as well as preparation. Calling up ships and personnel visibly demonstrates that a government takes a crisis seriously and may encourage negotiation before fighting begins. In a wider conflict, older frigates or destroyers could protect lower-threat convoy routes and release the newest escorts for the North Atlantic or other demanding theaters. A ship with a gun, an anti-submarine helicopter, and limited defensive weapons may be entirely adequate for a secondary route even if it is unsuited to the most dangerous operating area. The argument connects reserve depth to both crisis signaling and the efficient allocation of scarce modern escorts.

evidence.note: The lecture links prewar activation to deterrence and describes secondary-route convoy escort roles.

segments.title: Extra Type 45 hulls spread development cost and create depth
segments.summary: The Type 45 example links reserve depth to procurement economics: a larger production run could spread development cost while placing some new hulls in ordinary.
segments.body: A large fleet does not require every ship to remain fully commissioned in peacetime. Type 45 development costs were ultimately spread across six hulls rather than the larger force once contemplated. Building additional ships would have reduced the development-cost share attributed to each unit, even if some entered ordinary instead of active service. Newspaper criticism might focus on days at sea, but a reserve hull's purpose would be readiness for crew transfer, refit substitution, or mobilisation. This example connects reserve policy to production continuity and force-structure resilience rather than treating mothballing as wasted procurement.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke discusses the proposed Type 45 force, development cost spread across six instead of twelve hulls, and the option of keeping additional new ships in ordinary.

segments.title: Ships in ordinary absorb refit delays
segments.summary: A partly crewed reserve could absorb refit delays, exchange hulls with active crews, and expand wartime strength without keeping every ship commissioned in peacetime.
segments.body: The Type 45 hypothetical keeps additional hulls in ordinary with small care-and-maintenance crews. When an active destroyer entered a major refit, its crew could transfer to a ready reserve hull and preserve the number of ships available for operations. Wartime activation would combine personnel with prior Type 45 experience, the caretaker crew, and reservists, while some shore billets could be backfilled. The arrangement would also provide a replacement when damage or an unexpectedly long refit removed an active ship. Reserve hulls therefore create options and higher operational tempo without requiring every destroyer to carry a full peacetime crew.

evidence.note: The transcript develops a nine-ship Type 45 example with six active and three in ordinary.

segments.title: HMS Revenge finds a bombardment role
segments.summary: The old Royal Sovereign-class battleship became a useful coastal-bombardment platform without needing to join the Grand Fleet's battle line.
segments.body: Renamed HMS Redoubtable, the former Revenge received torpedo bulges and bombarded German positions off the Flemish coast. She was not expected to join the Grand Fleet at Jutland or defeat modern dreadnoughts. Instead, her heavy guns were matched to a shore-bombardment mission in which speed and modern battle-line protection mattered less. Flooding one side increased the elevation available to her guns, a practical adaptation that extended their reach against land targets. The episode shows how a navy could extract combat value from an obsolete battleship by changing both its role and the way it used its surviving capabilities.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke explains Redoubtable's torpedo bulges, deliberate list, and Flemish coast bombardment.

segments.title: Old battleships free the Grand Fleet to concentrate
segments.summary: Older battleships covered the Dardanelles and Channel approaches, allowing Britain's dreadnought strength to mass against the High Seas Fleet.
segments.body: Lord Nelson and Agamemnon remained dangerous enough to constrain Goeben near the Dardanelles, while other older ships reinforced the Channel barrier. Their service in secondary theaters allowed Britain's dreadnoughts and battlecruisers to concentrate in the Grand Fleet. The barrier force was unlikely to defeat the High Seas Fleet by itself, but it could impose damage and delay during a German attempt to reach the Channel. That would leave the Germans facing the pursuing Grand Fleet after already paying a price. Reserve and older ships therefore contributed to Jutland indirectly by protecting the strategic concentration of Britain's strongest ships.

evidence.note: The lecture connects secondary-theater battleships and the Channel barrier to concentration at Jutland.

segments.title: Why "pre-dreadnought" is a retrospective label
segments.summary: The "sovereign-style battleship" label avoids classifying ships solely by their relationship to HMS Dreadnought.
segments.body: The lecture uses "sovereign-style battleship" for ships commonly grouped as pre-dreadnoughts. "Pre-dreadnought" is convenient retrospective terminology, but it can imply that designers knew HMS Dreadnought was coming. The Lord Nelson class exposes the chronological problem because its ships were built alongside Dreadnought and commissioned after her. Opening here clarifies the vocabulary used throughout the lecture and the difference between a modern historian's classification and a contemporary design category.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke explains his preference for sovereign-style battleships and uses the Lord Nelson class's timing relative to HMS Dreadnought to show the limits of the later pre-dreadnought label.

segments.title: Presence duties and the World War II reserve shortfall
segments.summary: Even low-intensity presence work protects strategic relationships, while Britain's reduced hull reserve contributed to its severe ship shortage in 1941-42.
segments.body: A vessel that holds a distant station can prevent local problems from forcing modern combatants away from the decisive theater. A prolonged absence can weaken relationships, allow a regional problem to grow, and eventually compel the diversion of a first-line force. Older ships can cover those continuing commitments while modern units assemble for decisive operations. The abundant reserve hulls of 1914 contrast with the treaty-limited fleet of 1939. Britain retained many reserve personnel but reached the crisis of 1941-42 without enough ships for them to crew, demonstrating that manpower reserves and hull reserves solve different problems.

evidence.note: The transcript defines useful presence and contrasts British hull and personnel reserves across the wars.

segments.title: Old hulls become training infrastructure
segments.summary: Drill ships such as HMS Unicorn supplied recruiting and training space that expanded personnel capacity without new shore construction.
segments.body: Unicorn served in central Glasgow as a place where reservists could drill, maintain skills, and remain connected to the Royal Navy. Old hulls provided recruiting and training space in a recognisably naval environment without requiring new buildings ashore. HMS Victory and other stationary ships also mounted anti-aircraft weapons during wartime, but their larger contribution was institutional rather than tactical. They supplied the physical space needed to recruit and train the personnel who made fleet expansion possible. Such ships acted as force multipliers even though they were no longer fleet combatants.

evidence.note: The lecture uses Unicorn to show how old ships supported reserve training and recruitment.

segments.title: The Kriegsmarine entered war before its fleet was ready
segments.summary: Germany's 1939 navy provides a comparison in which its decisive submarine strength, surface-raider mass, and supporting logistics were not ready when war began.
segments.body: The Imperial German Navy's 1914 shortcomings resemble the Kriegsmarine's lack of readiness in 1939. Many of the U-boats that sustained the later submarine campaign were not in service until late 1941 or early 1942, after time had been spent building boats and training crews. The early surface-raiding force centred on Scharnhorst, Gneisenau, the Deutschland-class Panzerschiffe, and Admiral Hipper-class cruisers rather than a coherent, mutually supporting task force. Germany also lacked the stocked bases, logistics, and depth needed to sustain that force at scale. The comparison helps viewers separate impressive individual ships from a navy prepared for the war it actually enters.

evidence.note: The lecture compares German naval readiness in the two world wars, emphasizing the late arrival of much U-boat strength, the small surface-raider force, and missing logistics.

segments.title: Army-first funding left the Imperial German Navy without depth
segments.summary: Germany's land frontiers gave the army first claim on money and skilled people, leaving the Kaiser's fleet dependent on future expansion rather than a balanced existing force.
segments.body: Germany's geography required a very large army, and the service most directly connected to defending the land borders received first claim on funding. The overseas empire was strongly associated with the Kaiser's ambitions, so the navy struggled to compete for resources that did not visibly support the army. The result was "jam tomorrow": plans for future naval growth without enough present-day mass. Germany could field striking individual ships yet lacked the cruisers, destroyers, logistics, and reserves needed for a balanced maritime strategy. The argument shows why fleet depth is an institutional and budgetary outcome, not simply a count of capital ships.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke connects Germany's army-first funding priorities and the Kaiser's overseas ambitions to the navy's lack of balanced depth.

segments.title: The Brandenburg class shows why reserve roles must fit the ship
segments.summary: The slow Brandenburg-class battleships were poor North Sea interceptors but became more useful when reassigned to Baltic bombardment.
segments.body: The Brandenburgs were among Germany's earliest battleships and already had serious limitations by 1914. Two Ottoman examples had performed poorly against the Greek cruiser Georgios Averof, while the German survivors could no longer be assumed to reach their original 16.5-knot design speed. Assigning the ships to the Fifth Battle Squadron for North Sea coastal defence asked them to intercept British warships that could simply outrun them. The lecture's missile-interception analogy makes the problem clear: World War I visual detection did not give a slow battleship the long warning and calculated intercept point available to a modern missile defender. Baltic bombardment against Russian land forces better matched the old ships' guns and reduced the importance of speed. Reserve hulls are useful when planners give them missions they can physically perform.

evidence.note: The lecture reviews the Brandenburg class's age, speed limits, unsuitable North Sea interception role, and later Baltic bombardment work.

segments.title: How Britain sustained a broad naval reserve
segments.summary: Britain drew naval reservists from merchant shipping, part-time civilian volunteers, and former regulars whose retained service ties preserved experience and belonging.
segments.body: The Royal Navy could draw technically experienced people from the Merchant Navy, civilians who wanted part-time service, and former regular personnel. Volunteer reservists included professionals with careers and families who still valued naval work, community, or an additional income. Former sailors could retain useful experience as instructors or in other reserve roles even when injury or circumstance made regular service unsuitable. An informal support network helped people keep structure, status, and a connection to the service after leaving full-time duty. Those overlapping sources gave Britain a large mobilisation pool rather than a reserve dependent on a single recruiting channel.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies merchant seafarers, civilian volunteers, and former regulars as overlapping sources of British naval reserve strength.

segments.title: Army-navy competition shaped access to technical reservists
segments.summary: Germany's mechanizing army competed with the navy for engineers and mechanics, while a comparatively technophobic phase in the British Army left more technical personnel available to the Royal Navy.
segments.body: Both a mechanising army and a modern navy need engineers, mechanics, and other technically skilled people. Germany's large land force therefore competed directly with the Kaiser's fleet for the same reserve pool. The British Army between roughly 1905 and 1913 resisted technology across much of the service, although artillery, engineers, intelligence, and logistics remained important exceptions. That institutional preference harmed the army but made it easier for the Royal Navy to recruit the technical people required aboard ships. The consequence was visible in how old hulls were used: Britain employed them to free modern capacity, while Germany used them to compensate for ships it did not have. The comparison shows that reserve capacity depends on how a state allocates scarce skills across all its armed services.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke contrasts German army-navy competition for technical personnel with the British Army's comparatively technophobic prewar phase and their different uses of old ships.

segments.title: Germany's Jutland order of battle exposed a force-structure gap
segments.summary: Building dreadnoughts without enough cruisers, destroyers, or reserve depth forced Germany to place older Deutschland-class battleships in the main fleet at Jutland.
segments.body: Germany had sacrificed cruiser and larger-destroyer construction to fund dreadnoughts, yet still lacked enough dreadnoughts to match Britain. The Deutschland class consequently sailed with the High Seas Fleet at Jutland despite a top speed of about 19 knots and an armament of four 11-inch guns. Britain's Lord Nelson and Agamemnon were older battleships useful enough to constrain Goeben in the Mediterranean but were not needed in the Grand Fleet's main line. The contrast was more than a matter of ship-for-ship quality: Britain's reserve depth let it use older units in secondary theatres, whereas Germany used them to fill a numerical hole in its principal battle fleet. Germany was also trying to challenge a global maritime power while its economy depended on vulnerable sea lines of communication. Budget choices, supporting-ship shortages, and reserve weakness shaped the fleet Germany could assemble.

evidence.note: The lecture connects German cruiser and destroyer shortfalls, the Deutschland class at Jutland, British secondary-theatre depth, and vulnerable sea communications.

segments.title: Brandenburg-class guns outlived their battleship role
segments.summary: Even after the Brandenburg-class hulls ceased to be useful battleships, their heavy guns could be reassigned to railway artillery or proposed for allied ships.
segments.body: The surviving Brandenburg-class ships did not need to remain commissioned for their armament to retain value. Wörth's guns became railway guns, turning naval artillery into land-based heavy firepower. Brandenburg's guns were intended for transfer to the Ottoman Empire to support its ships, although the transfer did not occur. The example broadens reserve thinking from whole hulls to reusable weapons and equipment that can serve another mission after the original platform is retired.

evidence.note: The transcript says Wörth's guns became railway guns and Brandenburg's guns were intended, but not delivered, for Ottoman naval use.

segments.title: Obsolete cruisers become tenders and mine stores
segments.summary: Germany extracted support value from Irene-class cruisers by converting them into a submarine tender and a mine-storage hulk.
segments.body: Crew shortages made it impractical to send the Irene class to sea as cruisers, but their hulls still met essential support needs. Conversion of Irene into a submarine tender allowed an obsolete cruiser to sustain newer and more useful combatants. A sister used as a mine-storage hulk provided secure capacity without consuming a purpose-built ship. Keeping explosive stores aboard a vessel away from vital harbor facilities also reduced the consequences of an accident or attack. An old hull could therefore retain substantial operational value even when it was no longer worth crewing for combat.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke identifies the Irene class's tender and mine-storage conversions as useful wartime roles.

segments.title: Austro-Hungarian readiness came from planning for its likely war
segments.summary: The Austro-Hungarian Navy was modest in size but comparatively well prepared for its expected Adriatic missions, so readiness must be judged against strategy rather than fleet totals.
segments.body: Fleet size and preparation for the war a navy expects to fight are different measures. Austria-Hungary fielded a comparatively small navy, yet its submarines and balanced force structure were closely tied to likely Adriatic missions. Larger navies could still take on tasks that exceeded the depth, logistics, or ships available to them. The Italian fleet is the other contender in this comparison because it also built with its regional opponent in mind. This framing explains why very old river monitors could remain useful parts of an otherwise coherent wartime force.

evidence.note: The lecture argues that Austria-Hungary and Italy were relatively well prepared for their own expected naval missions despite not being the largest navies.

segments.title: Austro-Hungarian river monitors return to combat
segments.summary: The elderly monitors Leitha and Maros fought on the Sava and Danube, supporting occupations, river crossings, and operations through and beyond World War I.
segments.body: Leitha was about to demobilize when war preserved her service, and she soon fought on the Sava near Belgrade. A direct hit killed the crew inside her turret, but repair and rearmament returned the monitor to action in 1915. She later became a Danube Flotilla flagship, fought Romanian forces, and supported Austro-German river crossings. Her service continued into the postwar conflict against the short-lived Hungarian Soviet Republic and Czech intervention forces. This long combat record shows that age mattered less when a specialized shallow-draft hull still fit its operating environment and could be maintained for the task.

evidence.note: The lecture recounts Leitha's wartime damage, rearmament, river operations, and survival as a museum ship.

segments.title: Marceau becomes a floating workshop
segments.summary: Converting the old ironclad Marceau into a floating workshop gave French torpedo boats and submarines movable maintenance support.
segments.body: Early ironclad construction made Marceau easier to strip and convert than a later ship with more deeply integrated armor. Her large hull offered workshop space and had already supported torpedo-crew training before the war. As a floating workshop, she could fabricate or repair parts for torpedo boats and submarines whose machinery suffered constant wear in salt water. Mobile support reduced dependence on vulnerable or undeveloped bases and could move as operations shifted. The obsolete capital ship became logistics infrastructure that kept many smaller combatants ready.

evidence.note: The transcript explains Marceau's conversion and the operational value of movable maintenance infrastructure.

segments.title: Innovation creates a logistics burden
segments.summary: French shipyard experimentation produced ideas that other navies adopted, but incompatible machinery made workshops and fabrication capacity indispensable.
segments.body: French naval yards produced strong technical ideas, but political and industrial fragmentation made standardisation difficult. The Jeune École rested on a weak strategic premise, yet it stimulated technical ideas that other navies adopted. Continual design changes could leave a short run of boats with several transmission types, multiplying spares, specialised knowledge, and maintenance problems. A technically impressive craft contributes little if a distant squadron cannot obtain or fabricate the part needed to keep it running. Experimental energy is different from sustainable fleet construction. Innovative small craft still require robust workshops and logistics if they are to remain operational, which helps explain Marceau's conversion.

evidence.note: The lecture uses varying French torpedo-boat transmissions to illustrate the cost of weak standardization.

segments.title: Italy's second fleet strengthens the Adriatic blockade
segments.summary: Older Italian battleships and cruisers formed a second fleet whose very presence complicated any Austro-Hungarian attempt to break into the Mediterranean.
segments.body: Italy's maritime geography gave its navy a stronger claim on national funding than the Austro-Hungarian fleet could make against competing land requirements. Its industrial base and reserve depth supported a second fleet of older battleships and cruisers alongside the modern main force. The lecture lists Regina Margherita- and Regina Elena-class battleships, Pisa- and San Giorgio-class armoured cruisers, and supporting torpedo boats within that formation. The second fleet was inferior to the Austrian main force, but its ships were expected to fight hard and inflict damage. An Austrian breakout would therefore have to defeat one Italian formation and then face the other at reduced strength. That layered opposition helped sustain the Adriatic containment strategy even though the oldest Italian ships were unlikely to win a fleet action by themselves.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke explains how Italy's older second fleet added a costly barrier behind the modern fleet.

segments.title: Italian naval professionalism beyond the stereotype
segments.summary: Caricatures of Italian naval cowardice obscure aggressive professional crews and the later political and senior-leadership problems that constrained them.
segments.body: The caricature of Italian sailors as cowards obscures an aggressive, professional Regia Marina whose ships fought hard. Political and senior-leadership constraints complicated its operations in World War II. World War I helped the service accumulate experience that Germany's navy could not preserve in the same way after Versailles. Italy still faced constraints under the Washington and London naval treaties, but it did not undergo the same institutional rupture. Fleet performance, personnel quality, and political command need to be assessed separately rather than reduced to a national stereotype.

evidence.note: The lecture rejects cowardice stereotypes, describes the Italian Navy as aggressive and professional, and contrasts its interwar continuity with Germany after Versailles.

segments.title: Reserve insignia made part-time service visible
segments.summary: Distinctive RNR and RNVR markings advertised reserve service and strengthened group identity, even though common insignia could make reservists feel more fully integrated with regular personnel.
segments.body: Royal Naval Reserve and Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve personnel once wore markings that distinguished them from regular sailors and officers. Removing those distinctions can strengthen the idea of one navy and produce an immediate sense of equality. Visible insignia also gave reservists a distinct identity and showed the public that part-time personnel were serving on real operations. That visibility could support recruiting by allowing prospective volunteers to recognise people with civilian careers doing naval work. Reserve strength therefore depends partly on culture and public recognition as well as ships, training, and mobilisation plans.

evidence.note: The lecture discusses the former RNR and RNVR distinctions, the integration benefit of common markings, and the recruiting visibility lost when reservists can no longer be identified.

segments.title: Reserve fleets make wartime mass possible
segments.summary: Wartime fleets must preserve peacetime presence while adding combat, training, maintenance, and support capacity, making reserve hulls a source of depth rather than a substitute battle line.
segments.body: Wartime demand can require two or three times the peacetime ship total because routine commitments continue while combat fleets assemble. A navy must still cover distant stations, train replacements, maintain ships, and sustain fleets even while concentrating combat power. Older hulls can fill presence gaps, become stores or workshops, and support training. They release newer ships and shore infrastructure for tasks that genuinely require them. Each ship should be judged against its intended threat and mission rather than expected to provide frontline capability. The closing question asks viewers to design a modern reserve around lower-threat and support roles instead of assuming every stored ship must return to the battle line.

evidence.note: The conclusion summarizes reserve functions, wartime fleet scale, continued routine commitments, and the challenge of designing a modern reserve.

segments.title: General-purpose Type 23s released specialists for harder missions
segments.summary: The five general-purpose Type 23 frigates remained useful for presence, convoy, and task-group support even without the full anti-submarine fit carried by eight specialist sisters.
segments.body: The closing argument asks whether a ship needs defences against the most advanced threat when its assigned operating area is unlikely to face that threat. The Royal Navy's five general-purpose Type 23 frigates lacked some upgrades and the towed-array sonar fitted to eight anti-submarine specialists. They could still conduct presence and convoy duties or add a helicopter deck, Sea Wolf missiles, and a 4.5-inch gun to a task group. Using them for those jobs kept the specialist frigates available for missions that required their full anti-submarine capability. Honest role labels and differentiated readiness can make an older or less capable ship useful without assigning it to the highest-threat position.

evidence.note: The lecture distinguishes five general-purpose Type 23s from eight towed-array specialists and explains how presence and task-group duties released the latter for demanding missions.
